{{< include /_includes/mm-setup.qmd >}}

A medicinal chemist has just made a compound that binds its target beautifully in the assay. Then it fails: it will not dissolve in water, so it never reaches the bloodstream of the animal it is dosed to. Poor aqueous solubility is one of the most common reasons a promising compound goes no further, and it would be enormously useful to predict it *before* the compound is made. That is the question behind this episode and behind Chapter 2: **can we predict how soluble a molecule is from a few numbers that describe its structure?**

Before anyone fits a model, a careful scientist spends an hour looking at the data. That hour is {{< term eda "exploratory data analysis" >}} (EDA), and it has a checklist that is nearly the same for every table you will ever meet: shape, types, missing values, the distribution of the thing you want to predict, the distribution of each input, how the inputs relate to the target and to each other, outliers, duplicates. This episode runs that checklist on a classic dataset, using everything from [episode 1.3](03-pandas-dataframes.html) and [episode 1.4](04-visualisation.html).

::: {.bridge audience="bio"}
*Aqueous solubility* is how much of a compound dissolves in water at equilibrium, here expressed as a concentration in moles per litre. For a drug taken by mouth it is a gatekeeper: a tablet has to dissolve in the fluid of the gut before anything can be absorbed across the gut wall, and a compound that stays as a solid passes straight through. In the laboratory it decides whether you can make a stock solution at a useful concentration without a solvent that harms your cells. *Formulation*, the craft of turning a compound into a dosable medicine, has tricks to help (salts, particle size, carriers), but every trick costs time and money, so projects try hard to avoid insoluble compounds in the first place.
:::

## The data

The ESOL dataset was published by Delaney in 2004: 1,128 small organic molecules with a measured solubility, each described by a few simple numbers that can be computed from the structure alone. The file is not bundled with the course, so we load it with an idiom you will see again in Chapter 2: use the local copy if it exists, otherwise read it straight from the URL.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

ESOL_URL = "https://deepchemdata.s3-us-west-1.amazonaws.com/datasets/delaney-processed.csv"
path = Path("data/esol.csv")
esol = pd.read_csv(path if path.exists() else ESOL_URL)
esol.shape
```

1,128 rows and 10 columns. Column names first, because they are long and we will refer to them often.

```{python}
esol.columns.tolist()
```

The last-but-one column is the measurement we want to predict, the {{< term label >}}; in this course we call it the *target*. Give it a short name so that the long string appears once:

```{python}
target = "measured log solubility in mols per litre"
esol[["Compound ID", "Molecular Weight", "Number of Rings", target]].head()
```

The other numeric columns are {{< term descriptor plural >}}: numbers computed from the molecular structure, which will be the model's {{< term feature plural >}}. One column is special, `ESOL predicted log solubility in mols per litre`: it is the output of Delaney's own model, not a property of the molecule, and we will keep it out of the descriptor set. `Minimum Degree` is a graph-theoretic quantity that is 1 for all but 68 of the molecules, so it carries almost no information and we will drop it too.

Types and missing values next, exactly as in episode 1.3.

```{python}
esol.dtypes
```

```{python}
esol.isna().sum().sum()
```

Two text columns (`Compound ID` and `smiles`), eight numeric ones, and not a single missing value. That is unusual for real data and worth noting: this file has already been cleaned. Do not expect it elsewhere.

## What is logS?

The target is called *log solubility*: it is $\log_{10}$ of the solubility $S$ in mol/L, written {{< term logs >}}. A value of −3 means $S = 10^{-3}$ mol/L, one millimole per litre; a value of −6 means a micromole per litre, a thousand times less soluble. Each unit of logS is a factor of ten in solubility.

```{python}
esol[target].describe().round(2)
```

The median compound has logS ≈ −2.9, about one millimole per litre. The range runs from +1.58 (acetamide, so soluble that it dissolves at nearly 40 mol/L) down to −11.6, a difference of more than thirteen orders of magnitude.

::: {.bridge audience="chem"}
Why does everyone model logS rather than $S$ itself? Three reasons. First, the range: $S$ in this file spans from $10^{-11.6}$ to $10^{1.6}$ mol/L. A straight line fitted to $S$ would spend all its effort on the dozen most soluble compounds, because their values are millions of times larger than everyone else's, and would treat the difference between 1 µM and 1 nM as zero. Second, errors in log units are *relative* errors, which is how you think at the bench: being out by one log unit means a factor of ten, whether the compound is at 1 M or 1 µM. Third, the physics: solubility is governed by free energies of solvation and crystal packing, and free energy is proportional to the logarithm of a concentration, so the quantities that structure actually controls are additive on the log scale. The same argument applies to IC₅₀ (hence pIC₅₀), partition coefficients (logP) and rate constants.
:::

::: {.deep-dive title="Logarithms, factors and the geometric mean"}
$\log_{10} S$ is the power to which 10 must be raised to give $S$: $\log_{10} 10^{-3} = -3$. Adding 1 to logS multiplies $S$ by 10; adding 0.3 multiplies it by $10^{0.3} \approx 2$. Differences on the log scale are therefore *ratios* on the original scale.

Averages behave differently on the two scales. The arithmetic mean of logS in this dataset is −3.05, which corresponds to $10^{-3.05} \approx 0.9$ mmol/L. The arithmetic mean of $S$ itself is 0.39 mol/L, four hundred times larger, because a few very soluble compounds dominate the sum. The quantity $10^{\text{mean}(\log S)}$ is the *geometric mean*, $\left(\prod_i S_i\right)^{1/n}$, and it is the sensible "typical" solubility when values spread over many orders of magnitude. The same is true of the {{< term log-transform >}} of any right-skewed positive quantity: concentrations, counts, incomes, gene expression levels.
:::

## The distribution of the target

The first picture is always the target's {{< term histogram >}}. You are looking for the shape (one peak or several?), the width, and the tails.

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of measured logS for 1,128 compounds with a smooth density curve. A single broad peak between −5 and −1 centred near −3, a long thin tail reaching −11.6 on the left, and a short tail to +1.6 on the right."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.histplot(data=esol, x=target, kde=True, bins=40, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="measured logS (log10 mol/L)", ylabel="number of compounds")
plt.show()
```

One broad peak, roughly bell-shaped on the log scale, which is itself a sign that the log transform was the right choice. The left tail is long: a few dozen compounds below −7 that are practically insoluble. Keep them in mind; models tend to struggle at the ends of a distribution.

## The descriptors

Now the inputs. Six descriptors remain after dropping the two columns discussed above, and a 2 × 3 grid of histograms shows them all at once.

```{python}
descriptors = [
    "Molecular Weight",
    "Number of H-Bond Donors",
    "Number of Rings",
    "Number of Rotatable Bonds",
    "Polar Surface Area",
    "Minimum Degree",
]
esol[descriptors].describe().round(1)
```

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "A two-by-three grid of histograms, one per descriptor. Molecular weight is bell-shaped around 200 with a tail to 780; H-bond donors, rings and rotatable bonds are discrete and right-skewed, mostly 0 to 3; polar surface area is right-skewed from 0 to about 270; minimum degree is 1 for nearly every compound."
units = {"Molecular Weight": "g/mol", "Polar Surface Area": "Å²"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, descriptors):
    sns.histplot(data=esol, x=col, bins=30, ax=ax)
    ax.set(xlabel=f"{col} ({units[col]})" if col in units else col, ylabel="")
axes[0, 0].set(ylabel="number of compounds")
axes[1, 0].set(ylabel="number of compounds")
plt.show()
```

Two kinds of descriptor appear. Molecular weight and polar surface area are continuous and right-skewed. The counts (donors, rings, rotatable bonds) are integers, mostly small, with a few compounds far out on the right. `Minimum Degree` is, as promised, a single bar. From here on we work with the five informative descriptors.

```{python}
descriptors = descriptors[:5]
```

## Descriptors against the target

Which descriptors matter? Plot each against logS. Colour carries a third variable; because ring count and donor count are ordered quantities, use the sequential `viridis` colourmap rather than a categorical palette.

::: {.predict}
Before you run the next cell, decide: as molecular weight increases, does logS go up or down? And will the compounds with many rings sit above or below the others at the same weight?
:::

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of measured logS against molecular weight, points coloured from dark purple (0 rings) to yellow (8 rings). logS falls with weight in a broad band; at a given weight, compounds with more rings tend to sit lower."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(
    data=esol, x="Molecular Weight", y=target,
    hue="Number of Rings", palette="viridis", alpha=0.7, ax=ax,
)
ax.set(xlabel="molecular weight (g/mol)", ylabel="measured logS (log10 mol/L)")
plt.show()
```

Heavier molecules are less soluble: the cloud slopes down, though it is wide. At the same weight, the yellower points (more rings) tend to sit lower than the purple ones (few rings). (Because the `hue` column is numeric, seaborn treats colour as a continuous scale and lists only a few representative values in the legend; the full scale runs from 0 to 8 rings.) Rings, particularly aromatic ones, make a molecule flat and rigid and good at packing into a crystal, and they contribute little polarity.

Now polar surface area, coloured by the number of hydrogen-bond donors. Both are measures of how much of the molecule can interact with water.

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of measured logS against polar surface area, coloured by number of H-bond donors from purple (0) to yellow (11). The cloud is wide and only slightly rising; compounds with zero donors spread over the full range of logS at low polar surface area."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(
    data=esol, x="Polar Surface Area", y=target,
    hue="Number of H-Bond Donors", palette="viridis", alpha=0.7, ax=ax,
)
ax.set(xlabel="polar surface area (Å²)", ylabel="measured logS (log10 mol/L)")
plt.show()
```

The relationship is far weaker. Polar molecules are, on average, slightly more soluble, but the band is wide and the most insoluble compounds in the file all have polar surface area near zero without being distinguishable from many soluble ones. Polarity helps; its absence does not condemn a molecule by itself.

::: {.bridge audience="chem"}
Nothing in these plots will surprise you: the "general solubility equation" says that logS falls with the melting point and with logP, and both are driven by size, rigidity and lipophilicity. The point of the exercise is different. We are checking what a model could learn *from these five numbers alone*, with no logP and no melting point. Molecular weight and ring count are standing in for lipophilicity, imperfectly. That is why the linear model in Chapter 2 will reach only about $R^2 \approx 0.7$, and why Part II spends so much time on better representations of a molecule.
:::

## Correlations

A {{< term correlation >}} heatmap puts a number on every pairwise relationship, including those between the descriptors themselves. Short labels make the plot readable; `rename` with a dictionary does that without touching the original table.

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "A six-by-six heatmap of Pearson correlations between the five descriptors and logS. logS correlates −0.64 with molecular weight and −0.51 with rings, +0.21 with H-bond donors and +0.12 with polar surface area. Among descriptors, weight and rings correlate at 0.65 and donors with polar surface area at 0.76."
short = {
    "Molecular Weight": "weight",
    "Number of H-Bond Donors": "H-bond donors",
    "Number of Rings": "rings",
    "Number of Rotatable Bonds": "rotatable bonds",
    "Polar Surface Area": "polar surface area",
    target: "logS",
}
corr = esol[descriptors + [target]].rename(columns=short).corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.2))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", vmin=-1, vmax=1, cmap="vlag", ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Pearson correlation, ESOL descriptors and logS")
plt.show()
```

Read the last row. Molecular weight (−0.64) and ring count (−0.51) are the strongest single predictors of logS; rotatable bonds (−0.24) and the two polarity descriptors (+0.21, +0.12) are weak. Now read the rest. Weight and rings correlate at 0.65, so they partly carry the same information; donors and polar surface area correlate at 0.76, for the obvious reason that donor groups are polar. When two inputs say nearly the same thing, a model gains less from the second than its correlation with the target suggests. You will meet this again under the name *collinearity* in [episode 2.4](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html).

::: {.pitfall title="Correlation measures lines"}
Pearson's $r$ measures how well a straight line describes the relationship. A descriptor that affects solubility strongly but non-linearly, say with a threshold, can have a small $r$ and still be the most useful input for a flexible model. The scatter plots are the check: look for curves, clusters and thresholds that a single number cannot express.
:::

## Outliers: the extremes, by name

The ends of the target distribution deserve names. `nlargest` and `nsmallest` sort on one column and keep the top rows, and because the file carries a compound name and a structure, you can judge each one.

```{python}
esol.nlargest(5, target)[["Compound ID", "smiles", target]]
```

```{python}
esol.nsmallest(5, target)[["Compound ID", "smiles", target]]
```

The most soluble compounds are tiny and polar: acetamide, methanol, methyl hydrazine, glycerol. The least soluble are large, flat molecules made only of carbon and chlorine: a biphenyl with all ten positions chlorinated at the bottom, then coronene and benzo[ghi]perylene, which are sheets of fused benzene rings. Every one of them is chemically reasonable. An {{< term outlier >}} that makes sense is a real observation at the edge of the range, and it stays in. The time to drop a row is when it does not make sense: a logS of +5, a molecular weight of 3, a name that belongs to a different structure.

## Duplicates

A dataset assembled from the literature often contains the same molecule twice, sometimes with two different measured values. For a model that is a problem twice over: the duplicate rows get double weight, and if one copy ends up in the training set and the other in the test set, the model is tested on a molecule it has memorised. The {{< term duplicate >}} check is one line per column.

```{python}
print("duplicated SMILES:", esol["smiles"].duplicated().sum())
print("duplicated names: ", esol["Compound ID"].duplicated().sum())
```

None of either. That is reassuring but not conclusive, as the next section explains.

## The `smiles` column

What is in that last column? Plain text.

```{python}
esol["smiles"].head()
```

Each string is a {{< term smiles "SMILES" >}} representation of the molecule: atoms as their element symbols, bonds implied by adjacency, branches in parentheses, ring closures as matching digits, aromatic atoms in lower case. `CO` is methanol and `c1ccsc1` is thiophene. Every descriptor in this file was computed from the string in this column, and nothing else about the molecule is stored.

::: {.note title="Coming in Chapter 5"}
For now the `smiles` column is a label you can read but not compute with. In Chapter 5 you will parse these strings with RDKit, draw the molecules, and compute molecular weight, ring count, polar surface area and hundreds of other descriptors yourself, which is how you will build features for molecules that have *no* ready-made table. RDKit also answers the duplicate question properly: it converts every string to a canonical form, so that two different spellings of the same molecule become identical. Without it, `duplicated()` compares spellings, not molecules.
:::

## Framing the question

The EDA has told you what a model is up against. The target is well behaved on the log scale but spans thirteen orders of magnitude, with a thin insoluble tail. Two descriptors carry most of the linear signal and are partly redundant with each other; two more carry a weak signal of the opposite sign. The extremes are real molecules, not errors. There are no missing values and no exact duplicates.

So, the question for Chapter 2: **given a molecule's weight, hydrogen-bond donors, rings, rotatable bonds and polar surface area, how accurately can we predict its logS, and how would we know?** The first part is a regression problem. The second part, knowing, is what [episode 2.3](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/03-evaluating-models.html) is about, and the whole chapter begins with [episode 2.1](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/01-what-is-machine-learning.html), which sets out what "learning from data" means.

::: {.discussion}
You have only five descriptors. Based on the plots, which single additional number about a molecule would you most like to have, and why? (Chemists: argue for or against logP. Biologists and mathematicians: what property of the *shape* of the molecule might matter?)
:::


## Exercises

::: {.challenge level=1 title="The strongest descriptor"}
Without reading the number off the heatmap, compute the correlation of each of the five descriptors with logS and sort the result. Which descriptor is most strongly related to solubility, and in which direction? Is the sign what you expected?

:::: {.solution}
```{python}
esol[descriptors].corrwith(esol[target]).sort_values().round(3)
```

`corrwith` correlates every column of the left-hand frame with the single Series on the right. Molecular weight has the largest magnitude, about −0.64: heavier molecules are less soluble. The sign is negative because the dominant effect of adding atoms to a small organic molecule is adding non-polar surface, which water does not like. Ring count comes next, also negative. Note that `sort_values()` sorts from most negative to most positive, so the strongest *negative* correlation is at the top and the strongest *positive* one at the bottom; sort by `abs()` if you want magnitude only.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=2 title="Five scatter plots at once"}
Draw a 2 × 3 grid of scatter plots of logS against each of the five descriptors, with `alpha=0.4`, labelled axes and the empty sixth panel removed with `fig.delaxes(axes[1, 2])`. Which panel shows the clearest trend, and which looks like a cloud with no structure?

:::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "A two-by-three grid with five scatter plots of measured logS against molecular weight, H-bond donors, rings, rotatable bonds and polar surface area, and the sixth panel removed. Weight and rings show a clear downward trend; the other three are wide clouds."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(11, 6.5))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, descriptors):
    ax.scatter(esol[col], esol[target], alpha=0.4, s=14)
    ax.set(xlabel=f"{col} ({units[col]})" if col in units else col)
axes[0, 0].set(ylabel="measured logS (log10 mol/L)")
axes[1, 0].set(ylabel="measured logS (log10 mol/L)")
fig.delaxes(axes[1, 2])
plt.show()
```

Molecular weight shows the clearest downward trend, and rings is a staircase of the same shape: each extra ring shifts the whole column of points down. The counts of donors and rotatable bonds are clouds; most compounds have 0 to 3 of each, and within those columns logS covers the full range. Polar surface area rises faintly. `fig.delaxes` removes the unused panel entirely, which is cleaner than leaving an empty set of axes in a figure that goes into a report.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=3 title="Donors or no donors"}
Hydrogen-bond donors should favour solubility. Make a new column that labels each compound as `"no donors"` or `"one or more donors"` (use `np.where`), draw a violin plot of logS for the two groups, and compute each group's median. Is the effect large compared with the spread *within* each group? What does that tell you about using donor count as a predictor on its own?

:::: {.solution}
```{python}
import numpy as np

esol = esol.assign(
    donor_group=np.where(esol["Number of H-Bond Donors"] > 0, "one or more donors", "no donors")
)
esol.groupby("donor_group")[target].agg(["count", "median", "mean", "std"]).round(2)
```

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "Two violin plots of measured logS, for compounds with no hydrogen-bond donors and for compounds with one or more. The 'one or more donors' violin is centred about one log unit higher and is narrower; both violins span roughly eight log units."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.4))
sns.violinplot(data=esol, x="donor_group", y=target, hue="donor_group", legend=False, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="measured logS (log10 mol/L)")
plt.show()
```

Compounds with at least one donor are more soluble by about 0.85 log units at the median (−2.4 versus −3.3), a factor of about seven in solubility, so the effect is real and in the expected direction. But the standard deviation within each group is about 2 log units, more than twice the shift between them, and the violins overlap over nearly their whole length. Knowing only whether a molecule has a donor would tell you very little about its solubility; the descriptor is useful *in combination* with size and ring count, which is exactly what a multi-feature model is for. `np.where(condition, a, b)` is NumPy's vectorised if/else, and `assign` returns a new frame rather than modifying `esol` in place.
::::
:::

## Where this is going

[Episode 2.1](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/01-what-is-machine-learning.html) takes the question you have just framed and defines what a model is; [episode 2.2](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html) fits a straight line through these five descriptors; and [episode 2.3](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/03-evaluating-models.html) measures how well it does, honestly, on compounds it has never seen. Everything you noticed today reappears there: the thin insoluble tail is where the model's residuals will be largest, the redundancy between weight and rings is why regularisation helps in episode 2.4, and the `smiles` column, ignored until Chapter 5, is where the better features will come from.
